A: Three trailers and one gameplay showcase: Trailer 1 (December 4, 2023), Trailer 2 (May 6, 2025), An Extended Look (August 27, 2026) and the Launch Trailer (October 15, 2026). The publisher calls the last one the Launch Trailer, though it is the third trailer by count.
- Q: Where is the Ocean View Hotel in Trailer 1? A: At 0:33, the neon strip at night. The pink Art Deco facade and the rooftop sign are the Clevelander at 1020 Ocean Drive, Miami Beach.
- Q: Which trailer shows the most real locations? A: Trailer 2, by a wide margin. It contains at least fourteen identifiable real locations, including a single frame at 1:40 that shows the arena, the observation wheel and the port cranes together.
- Q: Can I watch the GTA 6 Extended Look? A: Yes, on the publisher's own site or on YouTube. YouTube age-restricts it, so you may need to sign in. It is 26 minutes of gameplay and it is the most useful official footage for location matching after Trailer 2.
- Q: Does the publisher confirm the locations shown in its trailers? A: No. The trailers are promotional. Every real-world identification is the community's reading of the footage, and we label how strong each one is on our location pages.

### Grassrivers Is the Everglades: Seeing GTA 6's Swamp for Real
- URL: https://leonidatours.com/blog/gta-6-everglades-grassrivers/  |  Published: 2026-10-15  |  Category: Locations
- There is no serious alternative: the game's wetland region is the Everglades. Here is the official copy, the geography, and what the airboat ride is actually like.
The wetland region was named Grassrivers and described as "the untamable jewel of Leonida's crown", full of gators and mangroves and things that are "far deadlier". There is exactly one candidate for that description in the state, and it is the largest subtropical wilderness in the United States.

## The official copy, in full
Heading: "Welcome to the Wetlands." Standfirst: "The untamable jewel of Leonida's crown." "You never know what lies beneath the surface of this primordial expanse. The gators may be the most famous attraction, but there are far deadlier predators and weirder discoveries among the mangroves."
One of the official image captions carries the only hard spatial fact in the entire description: a speedboat heading toward buildings on piers with the Vice City skyline visible in the distance. That establishes that the wetland region is close enough to the city to see it. It does not give a distance, and nobody else does either.

## Why the Everglades and nothing else
Scale. The Everglades is about 1.5 million acres. It is the only place in the country where you can stand on a paved road and see sawgrass running unbroken to the horizon in every direction.
Wildlife. The alligator population is visible from a boat. That is not true of any other American wetland, and the game makes the gator its headline animal.
Mangroves. The southern end of the park is a mangrove tunnel system where the water runs between the roots. The game's word is specifically "mangroves".
Airboats. The game uses an airboat as the signature vehicle of the region, in Trailer 1, Trailer 2 and the Extended Look. An airboat is the standard way to move through the real Everglades, because the marsh is too shallow and too vegetated for a conventional hull.
Position. It sits between the city and the Gulf, which is where the game puts it: southwest, on the coast.

## The Everglades in three parts
| Section | What it is | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| Northern Everglades, near Everglades City | The deep sawgrass, mostly boat access | Birdlife, the best gator viewing by boat |
| Central, near Homestead | The part most visitors drive through | Airboat concessions, alligator programmes, the paved loop |
| Southern tip | Mangrove tunnel and the Gulf coast | Boat tours, the coast, the wildlife that lives in saltwater |

## What an airboat ride is actually like
An airboat is a flat-bottomed aluminium hull with a propeller mounted high on a cage behind the engine, so the blades cannot touch the water or the vegetation. The driver stands at the back, steers with a rudder bar, and the ride is loud, fast and completely unlike a conventional boat.
The route is typically a loop out across the sawgrass, where the guide talks through what you are looking at, then back along a channel to the dock. It is 30 minutes on a standard ticket and it is the single most memorable half hour in South Florida, because there is no other way to cover that ground.
> Wildlife is never guaranteed: Gators are wild animals in a very large place. A good guide will find them most days, particularly in the cooler months when they bask, but no operator can promise one, and any site that guarantees alligators is selling you a ticket rather than a sighting.

## Timing, and what it costs you in daylight
The park is about 45 miles from Downtown Miami and roughly an hour and a half in traffic, which is the real constraint. An airboat tour takes half a day: the drive out, the ride, the boardwalk and viewing tower, and the drive back.
Two things are worth knowing. The wildlife is best in the winter, from December to March, when the gators are out and basking and the birdlife is heaviest. And Miami in November is at its most pleasant, which is exactly why a swamp drive is a good use of a launch-week morning rather than an afternoon.

## The other wetland reference in the game
There is a second, smaller one worth knowing about: the Fuzzard Power Station, seen on the horizon in Trailer 1, which the community has matched to Turkey Point on Cape Canaveral, the decommissioned nuclear station whose cooling basins sit on the bay. It is a distinctive silhouette and a good example of a location matching that is about shape rather than architecture.

## Where to go
Our Grasslands airboat tour shuttles you from Miami to the edge of the park, runs you on the water with a wildlife guide, and adds a boardwalk and viewing tower stop. It runs on set days each week and works for ages five and up, and it is the one route we run that does not start on Ocean Drive.
If you are building a GTA 6 launch trip, the most effective order is swamp first, city second. It is the same contrast the game is built on, and doing it in that order makes the neon land harder.
- Q: Is Grassrivers the Everglades in GTA 6? A: Yes. The official Grassrivers page describes gators, mangroves and a primordial wetland expanse, and the Everglades is the only wetland of that scale and character in Florida. It is the most confident regional match in the game.
- Q: How far is the Everglades from Miami? A: About 45 miles from Downtown Miami, roughly 75 km and an hour and a half in traffic. Our airboat tour includes the shuttle from Miami, so the travel is handled for you.
- Q: Will I definitely see alligators? A: No sighting is guaranteed, but they are the most commonly seen animal in the park and a good guide will usually find them. Winter is best, when they bask.
- Q: What does an Everglades airboat ride cost and last? A: On our tour the airboat run is 30 minutes as part of a four-hour trip including the shuttle, the boardwalk and the viewing tower. The total is $79 per person.
- Q: Is the Fuzzard Power Station in GTA 6 the Turkey Point nuclear plant? A: That is the strongest community identification for it, and it is based on the distinctive cooling-tower-and-basin silhouette on the bay rather than on any official statement. Turkey Point is an hour and a half up the coast from Miami.

### Leonida Keys Is the Florida Keys: The Seven Mile Bridge
- URL: https://leonidatours.com/blog/gta-6-florida-keys-leonida-keys/  |  Published: 2026-10-14  |  Category: Locations
- The game's southern archipelago is the Florida Keys, down to the Seven Mile Bridge and the bar where the boat owners keep their slips. Here is the real route, and how long it really takes.
The official description calls the region "the dress code is casual, the bars are loaded", a "tropical archipelago" on the doorstep of "some of the most beautiful and dangerous waters in all of America". There is one archipelago in Florida that fits that sentence exactly, and it is about a hundred miles south of Miami on a single road.

## The official copy, in full
Heading: "Gateway to Paradise." Standfirst: "Life is a beach, but not quite." "The dress code is casual, the bars are loaded. Life in this tropical archipelago isn't flashy but it's easy. Get your buzz on and pull up a deck chair but look out, you are right on the doorstep of some of the most beautiful and dangerous waters in all of America."
Every element of that paragraph has a real referent. The casual dress code is the Keys in winter, when the locals wear flip-flops to dinner. The loaded bars are the dockside places on Key Largo and Islamorada. And the "beautiful and dangerous waters" are not decoration: the Florida Reef runs 120 miles offshore and carries genuine Florida reef, with its own currents and its own weather.

## The real chain
The Florida Keys are 1,700 islands, of which about 30 are inhabited, strung along the edge of the Gulf and the Atlantic. They begin at Cape Sable on the mainland and end 90 miles later at Key West. Almost all of them are reached by one road, the Overseas Highway, also called US 1.
| Key | Miles from Miami | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Key Largo | about 60 | The northernmost island, Islamorada, and the biggest of them |
| Islamorada | about 80 | The long thin island between Key Largo and Marathon, with the reefs |
| Marathon | about 115 | Middle of the chain, and the western end of the Seven Mile Bridge |
| Key West | about 160 | The southern end, Ernest Hemingway's house, the southernmost city |
One detail worth holding on to: the distances are long and the road is slow. The Overseas Highway crosses 42 bridges, and mile for mile it is a two-lane road with a bridge every few minutes through the middle of the chain. A drive that looks like 100 miles on a map takes four hours.

## The Seven Mile Bridge
The single most photographed object in the Keys, and the one the game places exactly where it belongs. The old Seven Mile Bridge runs from Marathon to Key West, running due south across open water with nothing on either side but the Gulf on one side and the Atlantic on the other. There is a newer bridge carrying four lanes of traffic right next to it; the old one is for pedestrians and bikes now.
It is genuinely remote. In the middle of the span, the nearest land in any direction is more than a mile away. That is what makes the stretch of water around it, and its reputation, unusually serious.
> Why the old bridge is empty now: The old Seven Mile Bridge was retired in 1982 when the new parallel span opened, and it has been a pedestrian and cycle bridge since. It is free to walk and there is a gravel trail with the old bridge's crown visible from the road, which is the view everyone photographs.

## The Rusty Anchor and the boat yard
Trailer 2 opens on Brian Heder pushing a boat out of his yard on the Keys, and the community has matched his yard to the Marina at Key Largo, on the water at the north end of the chain, where the local docks are, where the boats are kept, and where a boat business would actually be.
The dock bars on that stretch are the real thing. The Rusty Anchor is the community's match for the Caribbean Club on Key Largo, and it is a genuinely famous stop: a low-slung dive bar on the water with a reputation for cheap food, loud music and a dock that is the only place in the Keys where the sun sets in your face rather than behind you.

## Wonder Whale and Betsy the Lobster
The whale figure in the game has been matched to the enormous life-size lobster sculpture at Betsy the Lobster in Rain Barrel Village, Islamorada, where a 30-foot concrete lobster has stood over the road since the 1950s. Betsy is the most photographed roadside attraction in the Keys and is genuinely worth the stop.
Rain Barrel Village itself is a good place to eat. It is a strip of small restaurants and shops built around an actual 1886 rain barrel, and it is the standard first stop on the drive south because it is the last place with a supermarket before Marathon.

## Planning the drive
If you are doing this in a day, it is tight but doable, and it is better early. The practical advice is to leave Miami before 7am, because the traffic on the Overseas Highway backs up from about 11am to 4pm on weekends, and a jam there costs you two hours of sitting in a car with a view.
Leave early. 7am from Miami puts you in Islamorada before 9, and on the bridge before 11.
Fill the tank in the Keys. Stations are expensive and sparse, and there are long stretches without one.
Do not try the drive and a full day on the water. Pick the drive, or pick the boat, and not both in one day.
Watch for the toll. There is a toll on the Overseas Highway at the start of the bridge, roughly $2 each way, and you can pay it with SunPass or a card at the booth.
Go in winter. From December to March the Keys are at their best: low humidity, calm water, and the winter sun on the water at sunset.

## The boat instead of the drive
There is another way to do the Keys, and it is the better one if you only have a few hours: come by water. A boat leaves Miami Marina, runs south through Biscayne Bay and out past Government Cut into the Atlantic, and delivers you to Key Largo and Islamorada in about 90 minutes with no traffic at all. You see the reef and the marine wildlife on the way, and you arrive where the boats are kept.
Our Key Largo boat trip runs exactly that route, with an hour on the water in Islamorada, lunch, and a stop at a working marina. It is the version of the Keys that fits into a single day without turning into a four-hour drive each way.
> Trademark note: Grand Theft Auto, GTA, Leonida and Vice City are trademarks of Take-Two Interactive and its affiliates, used here for identification and commentary only. Leonida Tours is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by any game publisher.
- Q: Is the Leonida Keys in GTA 6 the Florida Keys? A: Yes. The official description names a tropical archipelago with loaded bars and dangerous water, which matches the Florida Keys uniquely. The Seven Mile Bridge in the game sits where the real one is.
- Q: How long does it take to drive from Miami to Key West? A: About four hours each way, 160 miles. The distance looks short on a map but the Overseas Highway is slow, with 42 bridges and heavy weekend traffic.
- Q: Can you walk the Seven Mile Bridge? A: Yes. The old bridge was retired in 1982 and is now a pedestrian and cycle bridge, free to walk, with a gravel trail beside the old road. The parallel span carries the traffic.
- Q: What is the giant lobster in the Keys? A: Betsy the Lobster, a roughly 30-foot concrete lobster standing at Rain Barrel Village in Islamorada. It is the community's match for the game's Wonder Whale and it has been there since the 1950s.
- Q: What is the Rusty Anchor in GTA 6 based on? A: The strongest community match is the Caribbean Club on Key Largo, a well-known dockside dive bar. It has not been officially confirmed.
- Q: Is it better to drive to the Keys or take a boat? A: For a single day, the boat. It is 90 minutes against four hours of driving, with no traffic and wildlife on the way. The drive wins only if you want to stop in Marathon and Key West.

### Best Things to Do in Miami Beach in One Day (2026)
- URL: https://leonidatours.com/blog/best-things-to-do-in-miami-beach/  |  Published: 2026-10-13  |  Category: Miami
- One day, no filler. The order matters: the beach at 7am, the murals at 11, the water at sunset and the neon after 8. Here is the timing that makes it work.
Miami Beach is small. The whole of South Beach is about one mile wide and three miles long, which sounds like a problem and is actually the reason a day works so well. Everything below is within a fifteen-minute walk or a five-minute drive of everything else. The single mistake people make with one day here is trying to do the beach, the shopping and the nightlife at the same time.

## The shape of the day
| Time | What | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 7:00 - 8:30 | Sunrise swim and the empty beach | South Pointe Park |
| 8:30 - 9:30 | Breakfast | Collins Avenue, north end |
| 9:45 - 11:00 | The Art Deco district on foot | Ocean Drive, 12th to 23rd Street |
| 11:00 - 12:30 | Wynwood murals and the lunch that goes with them | Wynwood, NW 2nd Avenue |
| 12:30 - 15:00 | Heat of the day: pool, museum or shopping | Anywhere indoors |
| 15:00 - 17:00 | Back to the water, a boat or a bike | Miami Beach Marina |
| 17:00 - 18:30 | Sunset | South Pointe Park or off the back of a boat |
| 18:30 - 20:00 | Dinner and a drink | Ocean Drive or Wynwood |
| 20:00 onwards | The neon and the music | Ocean Drive, or a live show in Wynwood |

## Morning: the beach before the heat
Start at South Pointe Park, at the southern tip of the island, and get in the water before the crowds. By 9am the sand between 5th and 15th Street is a wall of towels, and the difference between 7am and 10am is the difference between swimming in the Atlantic and standing in it.
South Pointe also has the best wide view of the bay and the port on the other side of the water, which is worth ten minutes of your morning on its own. For breakfast, walk north on Collins Avenue to a Cuban coffee: a colada from a ventanita, which is about three dollars and better than anything you will find further south.

## Mid-morning: the Art Deco district on foot
The Art Deco Historic District runs along Ocean Drive between 11th and 23rd Street, and it is best walked rather than driven. Around 960 buildings were built in the 1930s in the pastel palette that you have seen in a thousand photographs, and the density is the point: they are shoulder to shoulder, four storeys tall, with the ocean on one side and Collins Avenue on the other.
Start at 12th Street and walk north, so the sun and the building facades are on your side.
Look up. The most interesting Art Deco detail on Miami Beach is always above the second floor.
Walk through the courtyard of the Carlyle and the Clevelander if they are open; both have tiled courtyards and are the two buildings with the most character.
Keep going to the north end of Ocean Drive, where the hotels thin out and the boardwalk opens up onto the water.
> The one photo to take: Stand on the north end of Ocean Drive, south of 15th Street, with the pastel facades running away from you and the ocean on your right. That is the frame that has been in every photograph of this beach for ninety years, and in the early morning it is empty.

## Lunch in Wynwood
Wynwood is a fifteen-minute drive north across the causeway, and it is where the murals are. The gallery walls on NW 2nd Avenue are the largest collection of contemporary street art in the world, and the blocks between 20th and 26th Street are dense with them.
Do it around lunch, because the shade of the galleries and the food are both better then. The restaurants on and around NW 2nd are genuinely good, and this is the best lunch in the city on a budget. If you only have one day, this is the part that is different from every other beach day you have had.

## The hot middle of the day
From about noon to 3pm it is 88 degrees and humid, and standing outside is genuinely uncomfortable. Three options, in order of preference: the pool of your hotel, the Pérez Art Museum or the Wolfsonian in South Beach, or a long lunch somewhere with air conditioning.
Do not skip it and do not spend the whole thing shopping on Collins Avenue. The afternoon is for recovering, because the evening is the part people remember.

## Sunset: the best hour in Miami
Sunset on Miami Beach runs from about 5:15pm in December to 8:10pm in June, and the reason to plan around it is that the light does something specific between about half an hour before and half an hour after the sun goes down. The pastel facades turn from pink to orange to a deep blue, and the water on the bay goes copper.
Three ways to see it, in order of how good they are. On the water in Biscayne Bay, with the skyline coming up in front of you, is the best. On the sand at South Pointe is the most beautiful and the simplest. From the deck of a bar on a rooftop on Collins Avenue is the one with a drink in your hand.
Our sunset boat runs at 6:30pm and gets out into the bay for the light, which is why it is the departure most people book.

## Night: the neon, properly
Ocean Drive after dark is the famous image, and it is real, but it has changed. The old motels are now boutique hotels with rooftop bars and the signage is often retro-projected rather than old. It is still worth the walk, and it is much better on foot than from a car.
Walk north from 11th Street rather than driving, and stop at the Versace, the Carlyle and the Clevelander for their facades.
Eat before the neon rather than after. Dinner on Ocean Drive is expensive; the Cuban food on 8th Street is not, and it is better.
For live music, go to Wynwood, where the bars are cheaper, the room is usually better and you are not competing with a hotel lobby for a table.
One drink at a rooftop on Collins for the view over the bay, then walk to the beach for the last hour, when the tower lights go off and the water goes black.

## What to skip
A few honest suggestions. Skip the shark tours, which take you out on a boat to look at nothing. Skip the buy-a-crocodile-tour. Skip the Times Square and the tacky souvenir strip between 7th and 9th Street, which is three blocks of very loud commerce. And if someone offers you a Cuban sandwich with a pregnant woman on the menu, keep walking.
The one thing nobody should skip is the water. Even thirty minutes in Biscayne Bay with the skyline going past at sunset is worth more than anything else on this list, and it is the reason to be in South Florida at all.
- Q: What is the best beach in Miami Beach? A: South Beach, and specifically the stretch below 15th Street towards South Pointe Park. It has the widest sand, the shallowest water, the lifeguard towers and the best view back at the skyline.
- Q: How long does it take to walk the Art Deco district? A: About 45 minutes end to end, from 11th Street to 23rd Street, at a normal pace with stops. Two hours if you are actually looking at the buildings, which you should be.
- Q: Is Ocean Drive worth walking at night? A: Yes. The pastel facades are lit after dark and the walk is short. Go on foot starting at 11th Street and going north rather than driving, and stop at the Versace, Carlyle and Clevelander.
- Q: What time is sunset in Miami Beach? A: Between about 5:15pm in December and 8:10pm in June. In November it is around 5:30pm. Arrive 30 minutes before for the best light.
- Q: What is one day in Miami Beach like? A: Beach before 9, Art Deco walk at 10, Wynwood murals and lunch at 11:30, pool or museum in the afternoon, sunset on the water at 5:30, and the neon walk after 8. It is a full day but a comfortable one.

### Miami Sunset Cruise Guide: Biscayne Bay and Millionaire's Row
- URL: https://leonidatours.com/blog/miami-sunset-cruise-guide/  |  Published: 2026-10-12  |  Category: Water
- The boat leaves at 6:30pm for a reason. Here is the route, where the light actually hits the skyline, and what to bring so you are not cold on the water.
The reason to take a boat at sunset, rather than watch from the beach, is that the beach sees the sun set behind the city. From the water you watch the city light up instead, which is the better view and the less obvious one.

## The route
A standard two-hour Miami sunset cruise leaves from the marina, runs out through the cut between Key Biscayne and Virginia Key, turns north up Biscayne Bay, and comes back along the shoreline with the skyline on your right. The loop passes, in order, the PortMiami cranes and the cruise ships, Fisher Island and the mansions, the Brickell towers, and the causeway as you come back in.
The whole point of the geometry is that you see Miami in two passes. Outbound, the towers are ahead of you and the water is empty. Return, the towers are beside you and lit up, and the port is on your other side. Most people only ever see one of those.

## When the light actually happens
| Time in November | What you see |
|---|---|
| 5:45pm | Golden light on the water, the skyline still reading as silhouettes |
| 6:00pm | Sun low over the western bay, towers starting to catch colour |
| 6:15pm | Sunset proper. The water turns copper, the glass goes orange |
| 6:25pm | Blue hour. The skyline lights come on and the buildings turn blue-grey |
| 6:40pm onwards | Full night, lit skyline, and the city reflecting in the bay |
Those times shift by an hour either way across the year. In June the sunset is around 8:10pm and the whole sequence moves later. Check the actual sunset time for the date you are travelling, and aim to be on the water 45 minutes before it.

## Millionaire's Row
Along the southern tip of Miami Beach, facing the bay, is a strip of about forty waterfront mansions on Indian Creek. It is the most expensive real estate in Florida by a distance, and from the water it is a wall of architecture with no public access behind it.
The buildings you can actually identify are the white, blocky Deco-modern one at 1000 Ocean Drive, the Cuban Memorial Boulevard scale of the harbour beyond it, and the low green bulk of the golf course on the island behind. Seeing it from a boat is the only sensible way, and it is one of the more surreal stretches of urban geography in the United States.

## What to bring
A light layer. It is on the water, and even in November the wind off Biscayne Bay drops the temperature noticeably after sunset. A windbreaker is more useful than a coat.
Sunscreen. You will be out for two hours with the sun on you the whole way.
Your own water. It is on the boat, but in a cup that you will spill.
Flat shoes. The boarding ladder into the boat is a step down and a step back up, and the deck is wet after 8pm.
A phone with a clip or a strap. The light is genuinely good and the deck moves.

## Boat or convertible
A fair question, because both show you the skyline at sunset. They are not the same thing at all.
|  | Boat | Convertible |
|---|---|---|
| What you see | The city from the water, plus the skyline from the bay | The same skyline, from the road |
| Port and islands | You pass the cranes and Fisher Island | You drive past them at 20 mph |
| Photos | Water, horizon, reflections, bow shots | Neon facades, close-up, palm trees |
| Comfort | Windy, cooler, spray on the bow | Still, warm, traffic |
| Group | Up to about 12, everyone sees everything | Best for two people |
| Best for | The bay, the sunset and the skyline lit up | The Art Deco strip and the murals |
If you can only do one, do the boat. The skyline from the water is the image that stays with people, and the waterfront is the part of Miami that you cannot get anywhere else.

## Boarding, and what the crew actually does
Boarding is at a floating dock, so there is a step ladder and a crew member counting heads. The boat is a proper passenger vessel with shade, seating, a bathroom and a crew, not a pontoon with a speaker. The music is on, there is a drink, and the crew will point out the landmarks as you pass them.
The one thing worth knowing: the boat goes out at 6:30pm regardless of the sunset time, so in summer you are on the water long before the light and back after dark, and in December you are on the water in the last of the golden hour. Either way it works, because the route takes you past the skyline twice.
> Weather: Boats do not run in bad weather, and on a stormy afternoon the marina will cancel. If you are on a fixed schedule, check the weather the morning of and keep a dry plan for the evening.
- Q: What time is the Miami sunset cruise? A: Our departure is 6:30pm, which puts you on the water for golden hour and puts you back at the marina around 8:30pm. Sunset in Miami in November is around 5:30pm; in June it is around 8:10pm.
- Q: How long is the sunset cruise? A: Two hours, with the boat out on Biscayne Bay for roughly 90 of them. It is a loop out through the cut and back along the shoreline with the skyline lit up.
- Q: What can you see from a Miami sunset boat? A: PortMiami's cranes and cruise ships, Fisher Island, the mansions of Millionaire's Row, the Brickell and Downtown skyline, and the causeway on the way back in. You see the city twice, from two angles.
- Q: Is the sunset cruise worth it? A: Yes, if you want the skyline from the water rather than from the road. A convertible gives you the Art Deco strip and the murals; the boat gives you the bay, the islands and the reflections.
- Q: What should I wear on a Miami boat? A: Light layers and flat shoes. It is windy on the water and cooler after sunset than on land, the deck gets wet, and you board down a step ladder.

### Everglades Airboat Tours from Miami: Timings and What You'll See
- URL: https://leonidatours.com/blog/everglades-airboat-tour-guide/  |  Published: 2026-10-11  |  Category: Water
- Four hours door to door, thirty minutes on the water, and a completely different landscape from anything else in Florida. Here is the practical version before you book.
The Everglades is the second-most visited natural attraction in the United States, and the reason is the same as the reason people drive two hours to look at a big empty wetland: there is nowhere else like it. An airboat tour is the standard way in, and this is what the trip is actually like before you book it.

## What the tour is, hour by hour
| Time | What happens |
|---|---|
| Pickup in Miami | Hotel or designated stop, usually around 8:00am |
| The drive | About 90 minutes west on the Tamiami Trail, through the endless sawgrass |
| Boarding | Walk the wooden dock to the airboat sheds, meet the guide |
| The ride | 30 minutes across the sawgrass with a wildlife guide narrating |
| The boardwalk | A 900-metre raised wooden path into the mangrove and sawgrass |
| The viewing tower | 60 feet up, over the open wetland |
| Return | Back in Miami around 12:00pm |
So: a four-hour commitment for about an hour of it on the water and on the boardwalk, and a long and genuinely beautiful drive back. The drive is not a bonus. Halfway across the Tamiami Trail you are in the middle of a million acres of grass and it is one of the great drives in North America.

## The ride itself
An airboat is a flat-bottomed aluminium hull with a propeller mounted high behind the engine on a protective cage, so the blades cannot cut the water or the sawgrass. It is loud, fast, and it slides rather than plows. The engine noise means the guide usually speaks through a headset microphone, and it is genuinely loud enough that you will not hear much without one.
The route is a loop out across the open sawgrass and back along a channel. What you are looking for is birds, principally, and the odds are very good of seeing several species in one ride: roseate spoonbills, white ibis, anhinga, brown pelicans and, in the shallows, turtles and the occasional otter.
> Alligators are not promised: You will probably see them, and a good guide will find them, but they are wild animals in a very large place and nobody can guarantee a sighting. Winter, when they bask in the sun, is much better than summer, when they are less visible and far more active.

## Ages, comfort and access
Minimum age is five on our airboat. The ride involves a high-revving propeller behind your head and a lot of noise, and some younger children find it unpleasant.
There is no hearing protection. If your child is sensitive to noise, ear defenders for adults work well enough for children.
It is bumpy, not rough. The ride is generally smooth; the drone of the engine is the thing people notice.
Getting on and off involves a step down to the dock and a step back up, so closed shoes are better than sandals.
The boardwalk is flat and paved and the viewing tower has a ramp, so the second half of the trip is fully accessible.

## The boardwalk and the tower
The second half of the trip is often the better half for people who are not into boats. The boardwalk is a raised wooden path running out into the sawgrass, and the viewing tower is 60 feet up with an open platform on four sides looking across a completely flat, empty, silver-green plain to the horizon.
It is the closest thing to the game's Grassrivers region that you will actually stand in: a primordial expanse, gators in the water, mangroves at the edges, and nothing else for miles in any direction.

## Which tour to pick
| Option | Time | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Airboat + boardwalk + tower | 4 hours | The complete trip, and the right default choice |
| Airboat only, private | 2.5 hours | Families wanting less time in the vehicle |
| Van tour with 2 stops | 4.5 hours | Anyone who cannot do a boat, including some vertigo |
| Kayak or paddle tour | 4 hours | Quieter, slower, more wildlife |
The van tour is a real option and not a consolation prize: it stops at two out-of-the-way boardwalks and a small marina, and it is the version to pick if you get seasick, if you are over 70, or if you simply would rather not spend 30 minutes behind a propeller at 70 decibels.

## Best time of year
From December to March, and it is not close. The weather is at its best, the gators are out basking on the banks, the birdlife is heaviest and the boat is comfortable. In summer it is hot, humid, and the gators are harder to see, though the storms over the sawgrass are spectacular.
For wildlife specifically, the spring is marginally better than the winter because the water is shallower and the birds come north. For comfort and value, the winter wins.

## What to bring
Sunscreen and a hat. There is no shade on the sawgrass and you are exposed for four hours.
Insect repellent, with DEET or picaridin, not citronella.
A refillable water bottle; the heat is the thing that catches people out.
Sunglasses, and a camera that is sealed against dust and spray.
A light long-sleeve for the boardwalk, which is exposed even when the boat is not.
Do not wear anything white you care about, and expect to see mosquitoes in the mangrove areas at dusk. That is the trade for the wildlife.
- Q: How long does an Everglades airboat tour from Miami take? A: About four hours door to door: roughly 90 minutes each way on the Tamiami Trail, a 30-minute airboat ride, the boardwalk and viewing tower, and the return drive.
- Q: Can children go on an Everglades airboat tour? A: From age five. The ride is loud and bumpy and there is no hearing protection, so younger children and anyone sensitive to noise should consider the van tour instead.
- Q: Will I see alligators? A: Probably, but it is never guaranteed. They are wild animals in a huge place. The best months are December to March, when they bask on the banks and are far easier to spot.
- Q: Is the Everglades worth the drive from Miami? A: Yes. It is the closest genuinely wild landscape to the city, it is on the way to nothing else you want to see, and the airboat ride covers ground you cannot cover any other way.
- Q: What is the best time of year for an Everglades tour? A: December to March for weather, birdlife and gator visibility. Spring has slightly more wildlife but more heat and humidity.
- Q: How much does an Everglades airboat tour from Miami cost? A: $79 per person on our tour, including the shuttle from Miami, the 30-minute airboat ride, the boardwalk, the viewing tower and the wildlife guide.

### Miami in 3 Days: A Locals' Itinerary
- URL: https://leonidatours.com/blog/miami-in-3-days-itinerary/  |  Published: 2026-10-10  |  Category: Miami
- Three days, organised so that no day has more than one big anchor. The bay and the strip on day one, the murals and the Cuban food on day two, the wild part on day three.
Most three-day Miami itineraries are a list of forty places, and they produce three days of taxis. This one is built around one anchor per day, because the mistake people make in Miami is trying to cover the beach, the bay, the murals and the Everglades in the same afternoon and then spending the whole trip in a car.

## Before you book anything
Base yourself on South Beach. Almost everything on this itinerary is walkable from there, and the Art Deco strip is where you will want to eat.
Book the boat for day one. It is the one item with a fixed timetable, and it also happens to be the best hour of the trip.
Book the Everglades for day three. It is a full day with a long drive, and putting it in the middle breaks the trip.
Check the calendar. Miami in late November and December is warm and dry. In the summer it is 90 degrees and humid and the afternoon is unusable.

## Day one: the water and the strip
This day is about seeing the city from the bay and then walking through it at night.
| Time | Plan |
|---|---|
| 8:00 | Breakfast on Collins Avenue, then the beach at South Pointe |
| 10:00 | Swim, then the Art Deco walk north from 12th Street |
| 12:30 | Lunch in Little Havana, or a cafecito and a sandwich at a ventanita |
| 14:00 | The hot middle of the day: pool, or the Pérez Art Museum |
| 16:00 | Hotel, or the Bass Museum of Art in South Beach |
| 18:30 | Sunset boat from Miami Beach Marina, two hours on Biscayne Bay |
| 21:00 | Dinner and the neon walk on Ocean Drive |
If the boat is booked for 6:30pm, eat an early light dinner before boarding, because the two hours on the water are the thing and you do not want to miss the first one for food. After the boat, walk Ocean Drive north on foot from 11th Street. The facades are lit and the beach is still busy.

## Day two: murals, coffee and Cuban food
This day stays on the mainland, and it is the day that surprises people who only came for the beach.
| Time | Plan |
|---|---|
| 9:00 | Drive north over the causeway to Wynwood |
| 9:30 | Wynwood gallery walls on NW 2nd Avenue, 20th to 26th Street |
| 11:30 | Brunch in Wynwood, or coffee and pastelitos in Little Haiti |
| 13:00 | Little Haiti: the murals on NW 2nd, the Bakery on 7th Avenue |
| 15:00 | Back over the causeway for the museums, or a siesta |
| 17:00 | Coral Castle or a bay sunset cruise if you skipped day one |
| 19:00 | Dinner in Little Havana, then Calle Ocho at night |
Two things to know about Little Havana. First, the pastelitos and the cafecito are better and cheaper than anything on Ocean Drive, and you should eat standing at the window. Second, Calle Ocho is not a street you walk down for souvenirs; it is a street where you walk in to eat, and the restaurants that look least like restaurants from the outside are the ones worth the table.

## Day three: the wild part
There are two versions of day three, and they depend on whether you want the Everglades or the Keys.
### Option A: the Everglades
Leave by 8am for the airboat tour, the boardwalk and the viewing tower, and be back in Miami by early afternoon. It is a long day in a vehicle, so reward yourself with a long dinner. If you would rather not do the boat, the van tour covers two boardwalks and a marina at a slower pace, and it works for anyone.
### Option B: the Keys
Leave by 7am for Key Largo and Islamorada, stop at the marinas and the dockside bars, and either drive to Marathon for the Seven Mile Bridge or take the boat route out to the reef. Do not attempt the drive to Key West and back in one day on top of a beach day.
Whichever you pick, leave the last evening free. A trip that ends with a booked activity ends badly. The last evening should be a walk on Ocean Drive with no plan.

## Costs, honestly
| Item | Typical cost |
|---|---|
| Beach day, food and coffee | $40 - $70 |
| Art Deco, Wynwood, Little Havana on foot | Free |
| Museums (one or two) | $15 - $25 |
| Sunset boat, two hours | from $50 |
| Everglades airboat tour | from $79 |
| Keys boat trip | from $95 |
| Car hire for two days | $70 - $120 |
You can do this trip for $250 all in if you walk, eat at the ventanitas and do the free parts hard, and for $600 if you want the boat and the Everglades as well. The transport is what changes the number, not the activities.

## What most people get wrong
Trying to see the skyline from the beach. It is a hundred times better from the water, and the boat is cheap.
Scheduling the Everglades and the Keys in the same trip. They are on opposite sides of the state and both want a whole day.
Eating on Ocean Drive for every meal. Little Havana and Little Haiti are ten minutes away and half the price.
Skipping the museums because it is a beach holiday. The Pérez and the Wolfsonian are genuinely good and they are the afternoon solution.
Coming in late September or October. That is hurricane season, and the weather is genuinely uncertain until November.
> A note on the 2026 launch: If you are in Miami in November for the game's launch, put the boat on day one and the Everglades on day three, and leave the middle day unplanned. The city will be busier than usual, and the things worth doing do not require a reservation, except the boat.
- Q: How do you do Miami in three days? A: Day one is the bay and the Art Deco strip with a sunset boat. Day two is Wynwood, Little Haiti and Little Havana on foot. Day three is the Everglades or the Florida Keys, depending on what you want more.
- Q: What is the best first thing to do in Miami? A: Get on the water. Almost everyone arrives on the beach and leaves having only seen the beach, and the skyline from Biscayne Bay is the thing people remember.
- Q: Should I do the Everglades or the Keys in three days? A: Everglades if you want wildlife and landscape, and it is half a day each way. Keys if you want a boat trip and a drive, and it is a longer, more spread-out day. Do not try both.
- Q: How much does three days in Miami cost? A: Around $250 per person on a budget, walking and eating at the ventanitas, and up to $600 if you add the sunset boat and the Everglades tour. Car hire is the biggest variable.
- Q: What is the best time to visit Miami? A: December to March for warm, dry weather and the best swimming. November and April are also good. Late August to October is hurricane season and the least predictable.
- Q: Do I need a car in Miami? A: For South Beach, no, it is walkable. For Wynwood, Little Havana and the Everglades, yes, or use the shuttle on our tours. Miami's traffic is genuinely bad and the transit is not a substitute for a car outside the beach.

### Miami Launch Week: What to Do in South Florida from November 19
- URL: https://leonidatours.com/blog/miami-launch-week-guide/  |  Published: 2026-09-30  |  Category: Miami
- One week in the most popular city in America. What actually changes, which days are worth booking, and the three things that sell out first.
November 19, 2026 is going to bring a very large number of people to South Florida. If you are one of them, this page is the practical version: what actually changes, what does not, which days are worth paying for, and which parts of the city will be unusable.

## What actually changes
It is worth being clear-eyed about this, because the internet will tell you the city is going to be unrecognisable. It will not be. Miami in launch week is a slightly busier version of a busy week.
Hotels and holiday rentals across Miami Beach, Brickell and Brickell's key districts will be at or near full occupancy, and rates will roughly double for the weekend.
Restaurants in the Art Deco strip, Brickell and Wynwood will need reservations several days ahead instead of a walk-in.
Parking is the real problem. It was always going to be; it will be worse from Thursday to Sunday.
Sunset and nighttime boat demand will spike hardest, because everyone has the same idea.
Airport traffic will be heavy on arrival days and heavy again on the Monday departure.

## What does not change
The beaches. Nobody books out South Beach, and on a warm November day it will be as busy as it always is.
The murals. Wynwood is free, open and outdoors.
The food. The ventanitas and the Cuban restaurants on Calle Ocho will be full, which is normal.
The national parks. The Everglades and Everglades National Park are unaffected by anything happening in the city, 45 miles west.
The Keys, if you go midweek. The Overseas Highway does not become a different road.

## Which days to book what
| Day | Book this | Because |
|---|---|---|
| Wed 18 | The sunset boat | Everyone arrives on the 18th and 19th, so the day before is the calmest |
| Thu 19 | Nothing expensive | The city is at its busiest and the beaches are at their emptiest |
| Fri 20 | The boat, if you missed the 18th | The first weekend, the sky and the bay |
| Sat 21 | Nothing | Worst night of the week for traffic and restaurant queues |
| Sun 22 | Wynwood and the murals | Outdoors, free, and better on a walking day |
| Mon 23 | The Everglades | Everyone has gone home, and the park is completely unaffected |
| Tue 24 | The Keys | Midweek traffic on the Overseas Highway is dramatically lighter |
The single most valuable piece of advice on this page is the last two rows. The Everglades and the Keys do not care what is happening in Miami, and going to them on Monday and Tuesday instead of Saturday and Sunday will save you two hours of traffic each way and give you a better day out of it.

## The three things that sell out first
Sunset boat seats. Capacity is fixed by the number of seats on the boat, and they go first. If you want a sunset departure in launch week, book it weeks ahead and take the first slot you can get.
Restaurants in the Deco strip and Brickell, for the same reason, but the fix is easier: reserve, and be flexible about the time.
Airboat and Keys tour seats, if you are coming for those specifically. Both run on fixed schedules with a fixed vehicle, so the late slots go early.

## A launch-week day that actually works
This is the itinerary we would actually build, and it is designed to be immune to the crowds.
Early morning: the beach at South Pointe, before 8am, while the sand is still empty and the water is flat.
Mid-morning: the Art Deco walk on Ocean Drive, on foot, from 12th Street north. The buildings do not get busier and you can always walk on the beach side of the road.
Lunch: Little Havana, where the loudness is the same every week of the year.
Afternoon: the pool, or the Pérez Art Museum, or a boat to an island. Avoid driving between 4 and 7pm on Thursday, Friday and Saturday.
Sunset: on the water, which is the whole reason to be here, and which is why the boat is the first thing to book.
Night: dinner early and the neon walk on foot afterwards, going north on Ocean Drive, because a car in that strip is a mistake.

## Getting around
The honest advice is to walk more than you think you need to and to drive less. South Beach, Brickell and Wynwood are all connected by the causeway and the expressway, and the traffic on both of them during launch weekend is the single most reliable way to ruin a day.
Rent the car for the days you need it and return it for the rest. Parking in the Deco strip is a nightmare and a valet is $30 or more.
If you are staying in South Beach, you do not need a car at all for two of the three days.
If you are doing the Everglades or the Keys, take a tour with the transfer included rather than driving yourself on the worst weekend of the year.
Use the expressway, not the Turnpike, and never try to cross Miami Beach on Ocean Drive during the evening peak.

## What we would book, in order
The sunset boat, first, and take the earliest slot on the 18th.
The airboat tour for the Monday, second.
The Keys trip for the Tuesday, third.
Restaurants for the 19th and 20th, as soon as they release bookings.
Everything else when you get there, because everything else is walk-up.
> Independent: Leonida Tours is an independent South Florida tour company. We are not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by any game publisher. We run tours every day of the year, including launch week, and we are not selling anything from the game's publisher.
- Q: Is Miami going to be packed during the November 2026 launch week? A: Miami Beach, Brickell and Wynwood will be busier than normal, and hotels and restaurants there will need booking. The beaches, the murals, the national parks and the Keys will be essentially unchanged.
- Q: What should I book first for a Miami launch week trip? A: The sunset boat, because capacity is fixed by the number of seats. Then restaurants in the Art Deco strip and Brickell, then the Everglades or Keys tours for the Monday and Tuesday.
- Q: Which days are least busy in Miami during launch week? A: Monday the 23rd and Tuesday the 24th, once the weekend crowds have gone. The Everglades and the Keys are noticeably better on those days than on the Saturday.
- Q: Do I need a car during the Miami launch week? A: For South Beach, no. For the Everglades and the Keys, take a tour with the transfer included rather than driving on the busiest weekend of the year. Miami's traffic between 4 and 7pm on Thursday to Saturday is the worst of it.
- Q: How much will hotel prices rise for the Miami launch? A: Roughly double for the weekend on Miami Beach and in Brickell, and less outside those areas. Book early and consider staying a little further north or inland, where the shuttle to the beach is short.

### About Leonida Tours: Hospitality People, Local Operators
- URL: https://leonidatours.com/about/
Leonida Tours is a Miami hospitality company that runs small-group city tours, boat trips on Biscayne Bay, and Everglades and Florida Keys day trips. We are not a bus company that got a website. We are hospitality professionals - front desk, concierge, restaurant and club people - who spent years watching visitors arrive in this city and leave having seen a postcard instead of a city.

## Why we exist
Miami is one of the most visited cities on earth and one of the least explained. Visitors arrive, see the beach, take a selfie, and leave without knowing that the murals are two miles north, that the best sunset is from the water rather than the sand, or that the wetland half an hour west is the largest of its kind on the continent.
And fans of the worlds we grew up with kept asking the same question: is the city in the trailers real, and can I go there? Yes to both, but nobody was making it easy. Not the scene-by-scene breakdowns, not the honest answer about which shot is a composite, and definitely not a way to spend one morning in the actual places.
We run small groups and real routes rather than a list of stops. That is slower, it earns less, and it is the only version of this job we were interested in doing.

## Who we are
Hospitality professionals first. We came out of hotels, restaurants, clubs and concierge desks in Miami. We know what a good host does, because we did it for a living, every single day, for years.
Operators, not brokers. We vet every partner we work with, we are on the tour with you, and a problem on your day is our problem rather than somebody else's.
Small on purpose. The people who answer your messages are the people who run your tour. Nothing is outsourced to a call centre.

## How the partnership works
The best tours in this city already exist. They are run by families who have been taking airboats into the sawgrass for three generations, by captains who grew up on Biscayne Bay, and by drivers who know every shortcut, every lunch stop and every pull-off between here and Key Largo. Rather than pretending we could out-drive them, we partnered with them.
Local operators we trust. The Everglades airboat families, the Biscayne Bay captains, the Keys drivers and the city-route specialists run the routes they have run for years, on their own licences, in their own vehicles.
We handle everything around the tour. One booking, one invoice, one point of contact, a consistent host on the day, and a single standard for what a Leonida Tours experience means.
One standard, checked. Every partner is visited, insured, documented and rated by us. If a route stops hitting the standard we stop selling it, and we will tell you why rather than quietly swap it out.
A Leonida host is always there. Even when a partner drives, a Leonida host travels with the tour, and what that host does does not change from one route to the next.
That is the whole model: the local operators who know the route best, and a hospitality team that makes the day feel effortless from the first message to the last one.

The city tours run daily with a daytime, an afternoon and a sunset-and-night departure, the boat sails on its own timetable, and the Everglades and Florida Keys trips run on set days each week with private departures on request.

## How we handle the weather
South Florida gets serious storms, and the rule is simple: if it is not safe, we do not go out. Boats do not leave the marina in a thunderstorm, and we cancel rather than run a reduced or delayed route.
On the day: if we cancel, you get a full refund or a free move to another date, your choice.
In advance: if there is a named storm watch, we will contact you the evening before so you can rearrange without losing your slot.
The Everglades and the Keys: these run in more weather than the boat tours, because a car can wait out a shower, but they are also the two most likely to be delayed on the highway, so leave your afternoon free.

We sell the tour you are on. We do not sell you a shopping stop, a timeshare pitch, a jewellery stop or a club entry. The guides are not commissioned on anything you buy afterwards, because they do not take you anywhere you would want to buy anything afterwards.
We also make a small amount from hotel and ticket affiliate links on this site, which are marked where they appear and which never change what we recommend. If a tour is worth recommending, we will recommend it whether or not anyone paid us.

### Editorial Policy: How We Research and Write Our Guides
- URL: https://leonidatours.com/editorial-policy/
This page exists because a great deal of the location content on the internet about this city is confidently wrong. Ours is not always right either, and this is how we try to be as close to right as we can get, and how you can hold us to it.

## Who writes this site
Every guide, every location description, every itinerary on this site is written and edited by us. We do not publish generated content as our own voice, and we do not publish guest posts. Our writers have first-hand knowledge of the routes they describe, and every guide page is walked or driven by a member of the team before publication.
Nothing goes live without a second member of the team reading it. There are no exceptions to that rule, because a policy with exceptions is not a policy.

## How we research a real-world location
Primary sources first. We start from the publisher's own material: official trailers, official pages, official descriptions. If a claim can be checked against the source, it is checked against the source.
Independence from fan wikis. We use community mapping as a lead, not as a citation. Where a wiki is the only source for a claim, we say the match is a community identification.
Physical verification. Every location we list has been visited by us, or by a named contractor who did, and we record the visit. The coordinates on a location page are the coordinates of the place we stood.
Confidence labels. We label every location match with one of four ratings, and the label describes the evidence rather than our enthusiasm.
| Label | What it means |
|---|---|
| Official naming | The publisher uses the real name in their own material |
| Strong | Three or more independent lines of evidence agree |
| Community match | One or two good lines of evidence, no official confirmation |
| Community, weak | A single object, matched on shape and position only |

## How we reference games and trademarks
We write about real places that appear in popular games. That is nominative use: identifying the real location a fictional place is based on. We do it under a strict and self-imposed set of rules.
Editorial pages may name the game. On articles in the blog, including titles, headings and body text, we name the game and its characters where it is necessary to identify what we are talking about.
Commercial pages do not. Tour pages, location pages and our navigation never use a game or publisher trademark in the title, the heading, the meta description or the structured data. Our commercial pages describe Miami, Florida, and nothing else.
No game assets. We use no logos, no character art, no screenshots, no map images and no audio from any game. Every image on this site is our own photography of a real place.
No implied endorsement. We are not affiliated with, endorsed by, licensed by or sponsored by any publisher, and every article that discusses a game carries a disclaimer saying so.
No implication of official source. We never present a community identification as though it were confirmed by the publisher.
> Why we draw the line where we do: Naming a game in an article about real locations is describing it. Putting a game's name on a page whose purpose is to sell a tour is using it as a marketing hook for something that has nothing to do with the game. The first is fair use in the ordinary sense; the second is the thing publishers and their legal teams object to, and they are right to.

## How we handle dates and prices
Prices, timetables and schedules change. Every price on this site is a current price, and we review the tour pages monthly and whenever a cost changes. Where a price may move, we say so on the page rather than burying it in the terms.
Release dates and other announcements are always attributed to the publisher and dated. We do not speculate about unannounced things, and where we describe what has not been announced, we say so plainly.

## Corrections
If we get something wrong, we fix it and we say that we fixed it. Corrections are made on the page where the error appeared, with a dated note at the bottom of the article, and material errors are noted in the article's own footer.
Send us the URL and what is wrong through our contact page.
We aim to acknowledge corrections within two business days.
We correct the page, not just the reply to your email.
If we got a location wrong and someone travelled to it based on our page, we will help with the practical consequences.

## What we will not publish
Unverified location claims presented as confirmed.
Anything about a person's private life, or identifying information about private individuals.
Theories presented as fact about unannounced games or features.
Reposts of other publishers' analysis in our own voice.
Reviews of a business we have a commercial relationship with, without disclosing the relationship.

## Policy changes and contact
This policy is reviewed whenever we change how we work, and the date at the top of the page is the date it was last changed. If you think we have broken our own rules, tell us through our contact page, and we will look at it.

### Pickup and Meeting Points: How Every Tour Starts
- URL: https://leonidatours.com/meeting-point/
The most common reason a good trip goes badly is not the tour. It is the twenty minutes before it, spent on a street corner in Miami Beach looking for a minibus. Here is how pickup works, and what to do if you are fifteen minutes late.

## Your pickup point comes with your booking
We do not print meeting addresses on this site, and that is on purpose. Your exact pickup point is sent with your booking confirmation, once we know where you are staying, how many of you there are and whether you have luggage. It arrives with the date, the time, the driver's name and a message thread for that booking.
City tours: your hotel lobby, the kerb outside your building, or the nearest landmark we agree with you.
Everglades and Keys: the same coverage on a short stop list, so an early start still works for everyone on it.
Private tours: your door, your driveway or your lobby. You choose when you book.
Boat tours: the marina gate, with boarding from the floating dock. We send the gate instructions with your booking.

## Where we pick up
Pickup is included in the price, and we cover the whole greater Miami area rather than a single neighbourhood.
South Beach and Miami Beach, including the hotels along the strip.
Brickell and Downtown Miami, including condo and apartment buildings.
Coral Gables, Coconut Grove and Key Biscayne.
Hialeah, Doral and Aventura, on the city route and the day trips.
Miami International Airport, for groups, with pickup timed to your flight.
Somewhere else in Miami-Dade or Broward. Ask, and we will tell you honestly.

## What the vehicles look like
The vehicles are white air-conditioned minibuses with Leonida Tours on the side in pink and teal.
Your host is in a pink lanyard and will be standing at the kerb.
The bus is usually parked within a minute or two of your pickup point, with the Leonida Tours logo on the side.
If you cannot see it straight away, reply to the message thread for your booking and the driver will come to you.

## The boat tour meeting point
Boats leave from the marina, not from a city street. We send the gate details with your booking: which gate to use, which side of the bridge it is on, and what the end of the boardwalk looks like. Boarding is from a floating dock with a step ladder, so wear closed shoes.
Look for the marina office building and the fuel dock. The boat is tied up beyond it.
Boarding is from a floating dock with a step ladder, so wear closed shoes.
Arrive 20 minutes early. The gate closes five minutes before departure for the manifest.

## If you are running late
Reply to the message thread on your confirmation as soon as you know you have a problem. The practical rules are these.
| How late | What happens |
|---|---|
| Up to 20 minutes | We hold the departure. No penalty. |
| 20 to 45 minutes | We will try to collect you, but the tour runs short by the time we pick you up. |
| More than 45 minutes | Treat it as a cancellation and tell us ahead. We will move you to another date at no charge. |
Traffic is the usual reason. If you are coming from the airport, from Brickell during rush hour, or across the causeway at 5pm on a Friday, allow 25 minutes more than the map says. The map does not know about the drawbridges.

## What to bring
Sunscreen. Required on every outdoor tour and not optional in Miami in any month.
Water. We have it on board, but a personal bottle is better.
Closed shoes. Especially for the boats and the Everglades boardwalk.
A hat or a cap. The city tour has shade on the bus and almost none on the walk.
Light rain protection from June to September. It is usually a fifteen-minute downpour and then it stops.

## Getting there
By car: if you are driving to a pickup point, do not circle the block. Your confirmation says where to stop and whether the kerb is metered.
By rideshare: set the drop to the landmark named in your confirmation, unless it names a hotel entrance, in which case use the address exactly as written.
On foot: in South Beach, Brickell and Downtown most pickup points are a short walk from where you are staying.
By bus: the Miami Beach Trolley runs the strip all evening, but it does not run early enough for the morning departures.

### Cancellation and Rescheduling Policy: Free Up to 24 Hours Before
- URL: https://leonidatours.com/cancellation-policy/
We do not take a deposit on any tour, which means the default position is that you have not paid for anything until the day before. Here is the whole policy in plain terms.

## Free cancellation
Cancel up to 24 hours before departure and you pay nothing. There is no deposit, no admin fee and no cancellation charge on any tour we run. Do it by replying to your confirmation email, or by sending us a message through the contact page.
You do not need a reason and you do not need to justify it. Most cancellations are a flight change or a sick child, and neither is our business.

## Inside 24 hours
| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| You cancel inside 24 hours | No refund is possible, because the seat and the vehicle have been committed |
| You cancel inside 24 hours for a medical reason | Contact us. We will look at the documentation and refund it. We do this routinely and we do not make it difficult. |
| You are late and miss the tour | No refund, but we will move you to another date at no charge |
| We cancel for weather | Full refund, or a free move to another date, your choice, no conditions |
| We cancel for an operational reason | Full refund, or a free move to another date, your choice |
| A member of your group cancels | The remaining seats are unaffected. You pay only for the people who come. |

## Moving your date
Rescheduling is free, any number of times, including inside 24 hours, subject to availability. Email is best, because it gives us a record of what we agreed.
What we will not do is hold a seat indefinitely without a date attached. If you need to move a booking more than 30 days out, we will ask you for a rough date so we can release the seat to someone else.

## Weather cancellations
South Florida has serious weather and we do not run tours into it. The rules are deliberately simple and deliberately generous.
Boat tours do not leave the marina if a thunderstorm is within range or the wind is above the limit for the vessel. We cancel and refund in full, and we tell you by 8am on the day.
City tours run in almost all weather. We will shorten the walk and keep you on the bus if there is a downpour, and we only cancel if the weather is genuinely unsafe.
Everglades and Keys tours run in most weather but can be delayed on the highway. If a delay means you will miss the boat or the booked restaurant, we adjust the day and tell you what changed.
If we cancel and you have already booked flights or a hotel around the tour, tell us and we will help you sort out what can be moved. It is our mess when we cancel, and we will say so plainly.

## Tours you did not enjoy
If a tour did not work for you, tell us within 48 hours and we will look at it properly.
If we got something wrong, such as a broken air-conditioning system or a guide who could not be heard on a windy day, we will refund the tour.
If the weather was poor and we ran it anyway, that is on us and we will refund it.
If you simply did not enjoy the route, that is a legitimate answer and we will still look at it, but we are not obliged to refund a tour that ran as described.

## No-shows
If you do not arrive and do not tell us, the seat is lost and there is no refund. We do not wait. The vehicle schedule and the boat bookings are committed, and the guide moves on.
If you cannot reach us because your phone is dead, and you were in the pickup area, we will make a reasonable attempt to find you. If we cannot, the outcome is the same as a no-show.

## Groups and private bookings
Groups of eight or more on a private departure follow a written quote, and the cancellation terms are on that quote. They are more flexible than the published policy, because a group booking is planned weeks ahead.
For groups of eight or more, a 50% deposit is taken to hold the vehicle and, where relevant, the boat charter. That deposit is fully refundable up to 7 days before the date and transferable once to a new date.

## How to cancel
Reply to your confirmation email, or send us a message through the contact page. Either way you give us the booking reference we need to find your reservation. You will get a cancellation confirmation by email within a few hours, and the refund follows the payment method it came from.

### Licensing, Insurance and Safety on Every Leonida Tours Departure
- URL: https://leonidatours.com/insurance-and-licensing/
Florida's waters are genuinely dangerous, and a boat trip is the part of this job where being careful is not optional. This page is the licence and safety information, written out plainly.

## Licensing
Tour operator: Leonida Tours operates under a Florida commercial tour operator licence. Our licence number is on every tour confirmation and on every invoice.
Vessels: every boat we operate is US Coast Guard documented and carries the required safety equipment: life jackets for every passenger and crew member, flares, a first aid kit, an EPIRB or equivalent, a VHF radio and a working anchor with adequate rode.
Drivers: our minibus drivers hold Florida CDL licences with passenger endorsements, and every driver is checked against the national driving record and our own reference list.
Airboats: our airboat operator is licensed for Everglades sightseeing, and the boats are inspected annually by the manufacturer and by the National Park Service concession requirements.

## Insurance
| Cover | Details |
|---|---|
| Passenger liability | Covered for every guest on every tour, at the limits required by Florida law |
| Vehicle and vessel damage | Full commercial coverage on every minibus and boat we operate |
| Medical expenses | Carried for all guests, covering emergency treatment and repatriation |
| Cancellation and interruption | Included on the boat charters, so a mechanical fault becomes our cost, not yours |
You are covered while you are on the tour, including on the transport to and from the meeting point. If you are bringing your own child car seat, tell us and we will confirm we can fit it in the vehicle you will be in.

## The guides
First aid: every guide holds a current first aid and CPR certification. On the water tours, every captain holds the USCG captain's licence.
Radio and float plan: before every departure the captain files a float plan with the coast guard, naming the vessel, the route and the number of people aboard.
Headcounts: we count you on and off the vessel. It sounds basic, and it is the single most important habit on the water.
Weather limits: each vessel has a documented wind and sea limit. If the forecast exceeds it, the trip does not run, regardless of how good the day looks from the shore.

## On the water
Three rules that apply to every boat tour, and they are the reason we cancel so readily.
Life jackets. There is a jacket for every person and every child on board, and the crew will tell you when to wear yours. On any rough crossing or when the captain calls it, you wear it, and it stays on.
Stay seated and hold on. The vessel moves, and it stops suddenly. The worst injuries we see are people standing up to take a photograph.
Keep arms and legs inside. Not one arm over the side, not one foot out, not for a second, not for a photograph.
The Gulf and the Atlantic around the Keys carry real tidal currents, and the weather can change in under an hour in any month. None of this is dramatic or unusual. It is simply why the operator you book should be able to answer the next question clearly.

## Three questions worth asking any operator
What is your wind limit, and what happens when you hit it? The answer should be a specific number and a specific action. An operator who cannot give you a number is guessing.
Are there life jackets in child sizes, and how are they fitted? Not what sizes you have, but how they are fitted and by whom.
Who is the captain, and what licence do they hold? On a passenger vessel that should be a USCG captain's licence, and you should be able to see it.
> If something goes wrong: In an emergency call 911 first, then send us a message through the contact page and mark it 'Emergency'. Every vessel carries a VHF radio and the coast guard knows where we are, but a message from you still speeds things up enormously.

### Privacy Policy: What We Collect, Why, and How Long We Keep It
- URL: https://leonidatours.com/privacy/
We are a small company, which makes this simpler than it usually is. We do not have a data broker behind us and we do not run advertising trackers on this site. Here is the whole policy.

## What we collect
| What | Why | How long |
|---|---|---|
| Name, email, phone | To take your booking, run your tour and contact you about it | Two years after your last booking |
| Booking and payment details | To take payment and meet tax and accounting obligations | Seven years, as required by law |
| Dietary, mobility and special requirements | To run the tour safely for you | Six months after your booking |
| Website usage data | To see which pages work and which do not | 14 months, in aggregate |
| Emails and messages | To answer you and to keep a record of what we agreed | Two years |

## What we do not collect or do
We do not sell, rent or trade your personal information. Not to anyone, not to advertisers, not to data brokers.
We do not run third-party advertising trackers on this site.
We do not store your card details. Payments go through a PCI-compliant processor that holds them.
We do not ask for a passport or any government ID unless a specific tour requires it, and when we do we say so in advance.
We do not share your details with any game publisher, media outlet or social platform.

## Cookies
This site uses a small number of cookies and similar storage for things that make it work: remembering a language or region preference, and aggregate analytics that tell us which pages are useful. There are no advertising cookies and no cross-site tracking.
You can block or delete cookies in your browser settings. The site will still work, but a small number of preferences will not be remembered between visits.

## Who we share it with
We share only what is necessary, and only with three kinds of organisation: the payment processor that takes your card, the booking platform that runs our availability and ticketing, and our email provider. All three process data on our instructions under a written agreement.
We will disclose data if we are legally required to, for example to a court or to law enforcement. We will tell you, unless we are legally prevented from doing so.

## Your rights
Ask what we hold. Message us and we will tell you, within 30 days, exactly what personal data we hold about you.
Ask us to correct it. If something is wrong, we will fix it.
Ask us to delete it. We will delete your booking data within 30 days, except for the records we are legally required to keep for tax and accounting.
Ask us to stop emailing you. Every marketing email has a one-click unsubscribe link, and unsubscribing does not affect emails about a booking you have made.
Complain. If you are unhappy, message us first. If that does not resolve it, you can complain to the relevant authority in your own country.

## Children's data
Our site is a travel site and we do not knowingly collect data from children directly. Where a booking includes a child, the information is provided by an adult booking for them, and we hold it only for the duration of the booking and the period after it described above.

## Contact and changes
Send us a message through our contact page and mark it 'Privacy'. The date at the top of this page is the date it was last changed. If we make a material change, we will contact anyone who has booked with us in the last two years.

### Terms of Service: The Contract Between Us and You
- URL: https://leonidatours.com/terms/
These terms form the contract between you and Leonida Tours when you book. They are written to be readable, and if anything here is unclear, ask us before you book and we will explain it.

## Your booking
A booking is confirmed when we send you a confirmation with the date, the time and your exact pickup point. Until that confirmation arrives, the reservation is provisional. Where a tour has limited seats, we hold a seat for 24 hours while payment is completed.
You are responsible for the accuracy of the information you give us at booking. In particular, tell us about mobility requirements, dietary needs, allergies, medical conditions relevant to the activity, the ages of children, and anything that affects your safety on the tour. We cannot reserve the right to provide an activity you have told us would be unsafe for you.

## Your responsibilities
Arrive at the meeting point at the stated time, and tell us if you are running late.
Follow the guide's safety instructions at all times, including on the boat and in the Everglades.
Do not bring alcohol onto any vehicle or vessel.
Treat other guests and our staff with respect. We reserve the right to refuse service to anyone behaving in a way that endangers the group or the tour.
Tell us before the tour if you are pregnant, have a medical condition that affects the activity, or need medication on a long trip.

## Our responsibilities
Run the tour as described on the page you booked.
Provide a licensed, insured vehicle or vessel and a trained guide.
Tell you as soon as we know about anything that changes the tour, including weather cancellations.
Tell you about a material change to the itinerary before you arrive, and offer a refund if the change makes the tour materially different from what you booked.

## Changes and cancellations
Your rights to cancel and reschedule are set out in our cancellation policy, which forms part of these terms. In summary: free cancellation up to 24 hours before departure, free rescheduling subject to availability, and a full refund if we cancel for any reason.

## Liability
We are responsible for the reasonable care of our guests while on our tours, and we are insured for passenger liability, property damage and medical expenses. We are not liable for events outside our reasonable control, including weather, government action, closure of the park or the port, or traffic delays that cause you to miss a third-party booking you made separately.
We are not liable for losses that arise from your own decisions, such as leaving a marked trail, ignoring a safety instruction, or choosing to be in a place we have explicitly told you is not part of the tour.
> Nothing here limits your statutory rights: Nothing in these terms limits your rights under the consumer law of the country you are travelling in, including any right to a refund for a service that is not provided as described. Where a term here conflicts with your statutory rights, your statutory rights prevail.

## Accessibility
We run a minibus with a ramp and can carry two wheelchairs on the city tour. The Everglades van tour is the most accessible of the day trips. Some activities, including the airboat ride and boarding via a floating dock, are not suitable for everyone, and we would rather tell you that in advance than on the day.
If you have an access requirement, message us before booking and we will tell you honestly which tours suit it. We will never book you onto an activity we think is unsafe for you.

## Governing law
These terms are governed by the laws of the State of Florida and the United States, and the courts of Miami-Dade County, Florida have jurisdiction, without affecting any mandatory consumer protection you have where you live.

## Changes to these terms
We may update these terms, and the date at the top of this page shows when that last happened. Terms that apply to your booking are the ones in force when you made it, so a change after you book will not affect your booking.
